studies.title: Warn Them Before It Comes
studies.meaning: The surah opens with the sending, and the instruction is a single verb with a deadline attached: warn them before a painful punishment arrives. Noah's reply repeats the assignment back in his own words and then reduces the message to three imperatives, worship, guard yourselves, and obey me. The commentators note the third, since obedience to a messenger stands alongside worship of God without being confused with it. Everything else in the surah is his report on how those three were received.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The whole chapter is given to Noah, and the commentators place it in the period when the Meccan opposition had hardened and the community was still small. No specific occasion is reported. Noah was known in Arabia through the older prophetic traditions and the Quran assumes the outline; what it supplies here is the shape of his calling rather than any new event from his life.

keyTerms.note: A verb for giving notice of danger in time for the hearer to do something about it. It presumes an interval, which is why the instruction arrives with a clause naming what the warning comes ahead of.
From a root for taking up a shield or putting a barrier in place. The verb describes protective attention rather than fright, so what is asked for is care in conduct and not a feeling.
The adjective means both making things clear and being unmistakable. Noah applies to himself the same two-word title the Quran elsewhere puts in the mouth of the last messenger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Warning in Arabia was a recognised office. A man who spotted a raiding party from high ground ran ahead of it stripped to the waist so that his message was understood before he could speak, and the Arabic word for such a man is the word used here. The image behind the title is not a preacher but a scout with a head start.
studies.didYouKnow: Noah describes himself with exactly the phrase the Quran later puts in the mouth of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in another surah, word for word. The same two words are given to other messengers as well. It is one of the shortest job descriptions in the book, and it is shared across the whole line rather than belonging to anybody in particular.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The three imperatives arrive as one instruction rather than as a sequence, and the third carries the weight. Obedience to the messenger is asked for in the same breath as worship of God without the two being merged, which sets the pattern for how a prophet's authority works throughout the Quran. The deadline in the opening line also makes warning a matter of timing, since the same words after the event would not be a warning at all.

crossReferences.why: Gives Noah's opening speech in another surah, in wording very close to this one.
Repeats the same imperatives from Noah, inside a series of parallel prophetic speeches.
Puts the identical phrase for a clear warner in the mouth of the last messenger.

studies.applyIt: Give one warning this week that you have been putting off because it will not be welcome. To a friend, a sibling, a colleague. Say it once, plainly, and then stop there. The instruction here comes with a deadline attached, and the whole value of a warning is that it arrives while there is still time to use it.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Deferred To A Stated Term
studies.meaning: The offer is made in two halves. Sins forgiven, and a deferral until an appointed term, and then a qualification that removes any comfort from the second: when God's term arrives it is not deferred. The commentators read the offer as an extension of life or of ease rather than an escape from the end. Then the scene changes without warning. Noah is speaking to God rather than to his people, and his report is two lines long: he called night and day, and the calling produced only flight.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is built as Noah's own account, which is unusual, and the commentators note that most of the chapter is in his voice rather than in narration. No occasion of revelation is reported. Its first audience was a community watching a message be refused, and a prophet's summary of a very long refusal was addressed to exactly that experience.

keyTerms.note: A term that has been specified rather than merely limited. The Quran uses the phrase of lifespans, of debts and of the world itself, and the naming is what makes it non-negotiable.
The verb for putting something back to a later date, used of debts being rescheduled. The same verb is then denied in the following clause, so the offer and its limit share one word.
A verbal noun for fleeing. Noah reports the effect of his calling as movement rather than as disagreement, which describes a social outcome instead of an intellectual one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Arabia ran on named dates, and rescheduling was a normal favour between merchants, since a term extended by a season could save a household. But everyone also knew the difference between a date a creditor could move and one nobody could. Noah's offer is framed in that commercial vocabulary, and so is the limit set on it in the very same breath.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for deferring appears twice inside a single ayah here, once as an offer and once as a denial. Arabic lets the repetition carry the argument on its own: what can be moved is your term, and what cannot be moved is the term itself. No further explanation is given, and the commentators treat the doubling as the entire point.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are offered and only one of them is open-ended. Forgiveness is stated without qualification, while the extension of time is capped in the next clause, which orders the two by importance. The report that follows then measures a calling by its result and finds none, without presenting that as a failure on the caller's part. The Quran records the outcome plainly and moves on, which is itself a comment on what a messenger answers for.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same offer in the mouths of earlier messengers, forgiveness and a deferral to a term.
States the same limit, that God defers no soul once its appointed time has arrived.
Supplies the length of Noah's calling as a figure, which puts a number on this complaint.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been given more time for than you expected: a deadline that moved, a result that came back better, a relationship that did not end when it might have. Name it once. This passage offers a deferral and then immediately says what cannot be deferred, and holding both together is the whole exercise.

studies.title: Fingers In Their Ears
studies.meaning: One ayah reports the reaction, and it is entirely physical. Every time he called them so that they might be forgiven, they put their fingers in their ears and pulled their clothes over themselves, then dug in and made themselves great, with the last word repeated in an intensive form for emphasis. The commentators note that nothing here is an argument. The refusal is described as a sequence of actions, two of them involving the body, and no counter-claim is recorded at any point.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators note the resemblance between this description and behaviour reported of some Meccans, who covered their faces or turned aside rather than answer, though no report ties the ayah to a specific incident. The surah is Noah's own account, and this is the single line in it that describes his hearers' conduct rather than his own effort.

keyTerms.note: A verb for drawing a garment right over the head and face. It shuts off sight as the fingers shut off hearing, so the two acts together close both faculties this account depends on.
From a root for binding something tight and holding to it. This exact form occurs only here, and it names continuing in a position rather than taking one up, a distinction English loses.
A verbal noun repeating the verb immediately before it, a construction Arabic uses for emphasis. The doubling makes arrogance the loudest item in a list that is otherwise quiet and physical.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A cloak was the one garment everybody owned, worn against sun and cold and pulled over the head for sleep or for privacy in a crowded space. Covering yourself with it in company was a legible act, the way turning your back is legible now. Noah's description would have been immediately clear to an Arabian audience as public refusal rather than as shyness.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names what they did to their ears and what they did to their eyes, and those two organs recur throughout the Quran as the standard pair for taking anything in. What is unusual here is that the refusal is bodily rather than spoken. Across a chapter made almost entirely of speech, this is the one line in which the audience does something with its hands.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Describing refusal as posture rather than as argument makes a particular claim about how rejection works. Nothing is answered; the channel is simply closed, and the closing is voluntary and repeated each time. That places the responsibility on an act rather than on a conclusion. It also explains why the surah turns to creation in the lines that follow, since an audience that has stopped listening to a warning may still be reachable through what it can see.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for covering yourself with clothes, there in an attempt to stay unnoticed.
Has the same gesture of fingers pressed into the ears, against thunder rather than against a call.
Records a different method of refusal, drowning the recitation out with noise instead.

studies.applyIt: Notice the physical thing you do when you are about to stop listening. Reaching for a phone, looking past someone, beginning to plan your reply. Everybody has one and most people cannot name theirs. Find yours this week in a single conversation, because this ayah describes refusal as something a body does before it becomes a position.

studies.title: Openly, Then Quietly
studies.meaning: Noah reports his method rather than his message: openly, then publicly and privately at once, three approaches in three lines. What he actually said turns out to be one sentence, an instruction to seek forgiveness, and it is backed by a name of God in an intensive form. Then the consequences he offers are entirely material: rain, wealth, children, gardens, rivers. Nothing about the next world is mentioned in the appeal.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah given over entirely to Noah, framed as his own report to God. No specific occasion is reported. Its placement in the Meccan period is not accidental: the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was calling a city that had begun to refuse him, and a surah about a man who called for centuries with almost no result was addressed to that situation.

keyTerms.note: A word for raising the voice so it carries. It is placed after a line about calling night and day, so the report moves from persistence to volume before it moves to method.
An intensive form of the word for one who forgives, implying repetition rather than degree. Noah offers it as a reason, so the argument is not that God forgives but that He does so again and again.
An intensive from the root for milk flowing from an udder, used of rain falling steadily. The image is not a storm but a supply that keeps coming, which is what a farmer actually wants.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain was the whole economy. A Meccan or a Bedouin heard a promise of steady rain the way a modern person hears a promise of secure employment, and the items Noah lists after it, wealth, sons, gardens and running water, are the full inventory of what a settled Arab family wanted. He is not offering an abstraction. He is describing a good year, repeated.
studies.didYouKnow: The same offer appears in another surah on the lips of a different prophet: seek forgiveness, and the sky will be sent upon you in abundance. Two messengers to two different peoples make the identical connection between asking pardon and rainfall, which is why the tradition came to associate seeking forgiveness with relief in material affairs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage joins two things usually kept apart: repentance and prosperity. Asking pardon is presented as having consequences in the weather and in the fields, which places moral state and material condition on one line rather than in separate compartments. It also shows a prophet varying his approach without varying his message, which the classical writers took as a description of what calling people involves: the sentence stays the same, the manner does not.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical offer in another prophet's mouth, adding strength to strength as a second consequence.
Gives the response he received, the detail immediately before this account of his methods.
Supplies the duration behind this report, which turns the persistence described here into a number.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person you have been telling something in the same way for years, and change the way rather than the thing. If you have been direct, try saying it once quietly and privately. If you have been hinting, say it plainly. Noah reports three methods and one sentence, and the variation is the part you control.

studies.title: Created You In Stages
studies.meaning: The argument changes tack. Noah asks why they hold out no expectation of dignity for God, and then supports the question with facts rather than warnings. They were made in stages. Seven heavens were made in layers. The moon was set among them as a light and the sun as a lamp, two different words for two different kinds of shining. And they themselves were grown out of the earth like a plant, in a construction that repeats the verb as a noun for emphasis.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The turn from warning to creation is characteristic of the surahs of this period, and the same word for layered heavens appears in another Meccan chapter close by in the order of the Quran. No occasion of revelation is reported. Noah is addressing an agricultural people, and the evidence he selects is the evidence available to farmers rather than to travellers or to astronomers.

keyTerms.note: A noun for the settled weight a person of standing carries. The question asks why they expect none of it for God, framing disbelief as a failure of proportion rather than of information.
A plural of the word for a stage or state passed through. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it makes a human being something assembled over time rather than produced at once.

The verbal noun placed directly after its own verb, a construction Arabic uses for emphasis. The line therefore says grown from the earth with a growing, insisting on the comparison rather than softening it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An agricultural community read the sky as a calendar. The moon set the months, and its phases were the working timetable for debts, markets and travel, while the sun set the length of a working day. Seed pushing up out of ground that had looked dead was the most familiar event of the year. Every item in this list was something the audience checked against their own fields.
studies.didYouKnow: The word given to the sun here means a lamp, a thing that burns, while the moon is given the plain word for light. The Quran keeps a distinction of this kind wherever it names the two together, using a word of burning or radiance for one and a word of illumination for the other, and the classical commentators drew attention to the pairing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument moves from warning to observation with no transition, which suggests the two are one argument in different registers. What is being asked for is proportion: given how they were made and what they stand under, a certain weight is owed. The comparison to plants also does something specific, since it makes human beings continuous with the ground rather than placed upon it, and the next ayat take that straight into burial and return.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical word for seven layered heavens, in another Meccan surah of this period.
Sets out the stages of a human being's making in detail, expanding this single word.
Names the sun a lamp and the moon a giver of light, keeping exactly this distinction.

studies.applyIt: Grow one thing this season, even badly. A pot of herbs on a windowsill is enough for the purpose. The comparison in this passage is not decoration: it asks a farming people to watch what comes out of the ground and draw a conclusion about themselves. Seeing something germinate once puts the line back in the register it was written in.

studies.title: Followed The Wrong Men
studies.meaning: The creation argument finishes with a round trip: returned into the earth and brought out of it again, then the ground described as spread flat so that broad routes can be walked across it. Noah's speech to his people ends there. The next line addresses God again, and the complaint is social rather than doctrinal. They disobeyed him, and they followed men whose wealth and children increased them in nothing but loss. Then one line about scheming, with an unusual intensive attached to it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators read the reference to men with wealth and children as pointing to the leadership of Noah's people, and the same pattern was visible in Mecca, where opposition was organised by the well-off. No occasion of revelation is attested. The word for the earth spread out and the word for broad passes both belong to the vocabulary of travel rather than of settlement.

keyTerms.note: The word for a rug unrolled on the ground. It occurs only here in the Quran, describing the earth by the household object a listener sat on daily rather than by any geographical term.
A plural for the open ways between hills. The word appears twice in the Quran and both times beside roads, so it names the gaps that make travel possible rather than the roads themselves.
An intensified form of the ordinary word for great, one step beyond the usual intensive. It appears only here, and it is attached to scheming rather than to anything admirable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Following a man was a formal act in Arabia rather than a mood. A person's alignment with a chief brought protection and obligations together, and switching was costly and public. Wealth and sons were exactly what made a man worth following, since the first bought support and the second supplied it. Noah's complaint names the two qualifications his people used and disputes only what they add up to.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this passage occur only once in the whole Quran: the one comparing the earth to an unrolled carpet, and the one describing the plotting as enormous. The second is an unusual grammatical form, an intensive built on top of an intensive, and the classical grammarians cite this ayah when they discuss it because there is nowhere else to cite.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The complaint identifies a mechanism rather than a belief. People did not simply reject a message; they followed particular men, and those men are described by their assets. That makes influence the operative thing and wealth its instrument. The line about increase is precise as well, since their possessions did increase them, but in loss, so the passage does not deny that money works. It disputes what it works towards.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same division from the other side, with the notables dismissing who had followed him.
States the pattern generally, that the affluent of a town are the ones who reject a warner.
Names the same arrangement of the earth, made a habitat with routes traced through it.

studies.applyIt: Name three people whose opinions shape yours most, and then ask what qualified them. Not in order to demote anybody. Just to see whether the qualification is judgement or something adjacent to it, like confidence or success. This complaint names wealth and family as the credentials Noah's people used, and the list is worth checking against yours.

studies.title: Do Not Abandon Them
studies.meaning: The leaders' instruction is quoted directly, and it is conservative rather than theological: on no account leave your gods. Five are then named. Noah adds that they have misled many. The section closes flatly and without any narrative of the flood at all: because of their wrongs they were drowned, then made to enter a fire, and they found no helpers apart from God. The commentators note how much is compressed here, since the entire deluge is given in three verbs and one denial.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These five names appear nowhere else in the Quran, and the classical sources report that idols bearing the same names were still known among Arab tribes at the time of revelation, several of them associated with particular clans. That connection is part of the point of naming them: a list of gods from before the flood turns out to be a list the first audience recognised from their own region.

keyTerms.gloss: do not on any account leave
keyTerms.note: An emphatic prohibition with a doubling particle attached, and it is repeated twice in one line. The urgency sits in the grammar, so the instruction reads as a campaign rather than as advice.
A plural for faults committed, distinct from the word for deliberate crime. The ayah gives it as the cause of the drowning without naming any single act among them.
The plural of the word for one who comes to another's aid, a central term in the tribal order. The line denies them exactly the resource the gods they were told to keep were supposed to supply.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Idols in Arabia were owned. A clan kept one, maintained it, and drew standing and income from the pilgrimage traffic it attracted, so abandoning a god meant dismantling a family's position and its livelihood together. The instruction quoted here would have sounded to a Meccan audience less like a creed than like a decision taken at a family meeting, which is roughly what it was.
studies.didYouKnow: Five gods are named in this ayah, and not one of them appears anywhere else in the Quran. The classical sources report that idols with those same five names were known among Arab tribes when the Quran was revealed, which means the list reads at once as ancient history and as a description of the first audience's own neighbourhood.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument the leaders make is not that their gods are true but that they are theirs, and the passage records it without answering. Continuity is offered as a reason all by itself. The closing line then compresses an entire flood into three verbs and supplies no scene whatever. What the surah preserves is the sentence rather than the spectacle, which keeps the weight on the reasoning that led there.

crossReferences.why: Names three other deities of the same kind, in a passage addressed directly to Mecca.
Records the same conservative objection, that turning many gods into one is a strange novelty.
Gives the flood scene this passage compresses, including a son who would not board.

studies.applyIt: Identify one thing you keep doing mainly because it is what your family has always done. Not in order to abandon it. Just to notice that the reason you would give, if pressed, is continuity and nothing else. That is the exact argument quoted in this ayah, and recognising it in a small case makes it visible in larger ones.

studies.title: A Prayer Without Exception
studies.meaning: Noah asks that not one of them be left on the earth, using a word that means a single inhabitant, and then gives his reason. If they remain they will mislead the servants of God, and they will father nothing but the openly wicked and the persistently ungrateful. The commentators handle this carefully. They read the second line as knowledge he had been given rather than as a prediction he ventured, and they note that the request comes at the end of a very long calling rather than at the start of one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Another surah reports that Noah was told nobody further from his people would believe, and the classical commentators read this prayer as following that information rather than preceding it. No occasion of revelation is attested for these ayat. The chapter presents the prayer as the last item in his report, after the account of his methods, his arguments and his people's reply.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form built from the word for a dwelling, used almost only inside a negation to mean not one inhabitant. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it is the strongest available way of saying nobody.
A causative from the verb for going astray, so the harm named is what they would do to other people rather than their own condition. The reason offered for the prayer is transmission, not punishment.
An intensive from the root that covers both covering something over and refusing thanks. Paired here with a word for the openly wicked, it names a settled disposition rather than a single act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Belief travelled through households in Arabia. A child grew up inside the practices of a clan, married within an alliance, and inherited a god along with a trade, so a conviction moved the way property moved. Noah's concern about what his people would father was not an abstraction about heredity. It described the actual machinery by which a religion passed from one generation to the next.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Noah uses for a single inhabitant appears only once in the Quran, and Arabic uses it almost exclusively inside a negation, so the word itself only ever means the absence of anybody at all. He also uses the verb to leave twice in this prayer, the same verb the leaders had used twice when telling their people not to leave their gods.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer is not for punishment but for an end to transmission, and the wording makes that distinction explicit. What is described as the danger is inheritance: not what these people are but what they would pass on. That framing keeps the request from being personal, and the commentators use it to explain how a prophet described elsewhere as patient across centuries could ask for this at the end. The reasoning is about generations.

crossReferences.why: Reports what Noah had been told, that nobody further from his people would come to believe.
Gives his prayer in another surah in a few words, as a plea for help rather than for removal.
Names the length of his calling before this point, which is the context the commentators supply.

studies.applyIt: Think about something you know you are passing on without meaning to. A way of arguing, an attitude to money, a manner around food. Children and colleagues both pick these up quickly. You do not have to fix it this week. Notice one, and notice that this prayer is entirely about what gets passed forward rather than about anyone's fault.

studies.title: Forgive Me And My Parents
studies.meaning: The last ayah is a prayer, and it starts with the man saying it. Forgiveness for himself, then for his two parents, then for whoever entered his house as a believer, then for the believing men and the believing women with no limit of time or place attached. Only after all of that comes the closing clause about the wrongdoers. The commentators note the order and the widening: the circle opens at one person and ends at everybody who will ever belong to it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a chapter that is almost entirely in Noah's voice. The commentators point out that his parents are mentioned nowhere else in the Quran, and that nothing is reported about them beyond this line. No occasion of revelation is attested. The reference to those who entered his house is read either as his own household or as the small group who came to him, and the sources transmit both.

keyTerms.note: A dual form, so both parents are named together in a single word. Arabic marks pairs with their own grammatical number, and the prayer therefore includes them as a unit rather than as two requests.
The ordinary word for a house. Commentators read it as his household, or as the place where those who accepted his message gathered, and they transmit both readings without deciding between them.
A noun for destruction that leaves nothing behind it. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it is the last word of the surah, closing a chapter that opened with a warning issued in time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A house in Arabia was a social boundary. Who came in, who was fed, and who was given a place to sleep declared alignments that everybody else could read, and a household that opened its door to an unpopular man made a public statement by doing it. The prayer for whoever entered his house as a believer names the people who had paid a visible price for coming.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where Noah's parents are mentioned, and nothing further is said about them anywhere in the text. The prayer also names four widening circles inside a single ayah, and the last of them, the believing men and the believing women, is a phrase the Quran uses elsewhere for the whole community across time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer's structure is its argument. Forgiveness is asked for in a widening series, and the widest circle is not defined by acquaintance at all, which extends the request to people the speaker could never meet. Placing his parents second matters too, since the request runs backwards in time before it runs outwards. The final clause about the wrongdoers is brief, and the surah gives its last word to ruin rather than to relief.

crossReferences.why: Gives Abraham's closely parallel prayer, for himself, his parents and the believers together.
Gives the short prayer for parents that the Quran teaches its readers directly.
Extends forgiveness backwards to believers who came before, in the same widening motion.

studies.applyIt: Say a prayer for your parents today, whether they are alive or not, and then add one person who once opened a door for you when it cost them something. Noah's last recorded words move outwards in exactly that order. It takes half a minute, and most people find the second name harder to produce than they expect.
